newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya alliance calls for fresh action to test Moi.
newsitem.headline: Kenya alliance calls for fresh action to test Moi.

text.p: An opposition-backed alliance unveiled on Thursday a series of "mass actions" in Kenya to test President Daniel arap Moi while welcoming talks with him on constitutional reforms.
The list of actions included a rally in Kenya's second city of Mombasa, centre of its tourism industry, on the Indian Ocean coast on July 26 and a national general strike and sit-in on August 8.

The steps were read at a news conference by Willy Mutunga, co-convenor of the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC), grouping all opposition parties, human rights groups and other bodies demanding constitutional reforms before elections.
On Moi's agreement on Wednesday to discuss reforms with the opposition next week and his agreeing with religious leaders on Tuesday on the need to review the constitution, Mutunga said:

"The NCEC position is that we welcome these meetings. We see them as talks about talks but they are not what we want. Talks about talks are all right as long as the end result is not lost sight of -- constitutional reforms."
"We will continue our programme of mass action," he said, calling on the government to take a series of measures including stamping out banditry and resettling victims of ethnic clashes.

"We warn Kenyans these 'talks about talks' can be used to divide and rule the reform movement," he added. NCEC members say Moi this week started a political offensive aimed at hijacking the campaign and splitting the opposition to head off violence.

Mutunga listed 12 days of "mass actions" in July and August "to test the government's good faith on dialogue" including an all-night vigil in Nairobi on Thursday night and a prayer meeting in a Nairobi park on Friday for the dead from clashes.
Riot police on July 7 violently broke up rallies in Nairobi and several other cities and towns and at least nine people were killed in the worst political violence in Kenya in seven years.
The July 7 violence, which closed down Nairobi, was followed by days of student unrest in the city, prompting the closure of two universities followed by the Kenya Polytechnic on Monday.
But Foreign Minister Kalonzo Musyoka said later on Friday Kenya was back to normal after violence last week and reiterated Moi's position that there was no time for reforms before the elections.
He said violence in the Kenyan capital and other towns last week had led to numerous tourist cancellations and planners of international conferences had been also seeking other venues.
But he said his message was "all is back to normal in Kenya and they should come". He gave no details of the cancellations.
The NCEC said if it did not get constitutional reforms as well as six months for them to take effect before elections it would disrupt polls across Kenya so they could not take place.
"Without reforms we are not going to have elections," said James Orengo, an opposition parliamentarian and NCEC member.
The constitutional reforms sought by the opposition would reduce the power of Moi, 73 and Kenya's ruler for 19 years. No date for the presidential and parliamentary polls has been set.
In his second apparent concession under pressure from the reform campaign, Moi said on Wednesday opposition parties would automatically be granted official licences for rallies in most cases.
But the NCEC said it would not even apply for licences, arguing Moi should dismantle the law requiring them because they ran counter to the right of free assembly in the constitution.
The NCEC on Thursday distanced itself from fiery Islamic preacher Sheikh Khalid Balala, saying it did not agree with his call this week for the burning of all voter registration cards.
